Joshua 1.summary: After Moses' death, the LORD speaks to Joshua, Moses' assistant, and commissions him to lead Israel across the Jordan into the land promised to their ancestors (Joshua 1:1-4). God promises that no one will stand against him and that he will be with Joshua as he was with Moses (Joshua 1:5). Three times Joshua is told to be strong and courageous, and he is told to keep the book of the law on his lips and meditate on it day and night so that he may act carefully and have success (Joshua 1:6-9). Joshua orders the officers to tell the people to prepare provisions to cross in three days (Joshua 1:10-11). He reminds the tribes of Reuben, Gad, and half of Manasseh of Moses' command that their fighting men cross armed and help their brothers until all have rest (Joshua 1:12-15). They pledge to obey Joshua as they obeyed Moses (Joshua 1:16-18).
Joshua 1.whereWeAre: Deuteronomy ended with the death of Moses on mount Nebo. Now God speaks to Joshua, Moses' helper, and tells him to lead Israel across the Jordan: "Be strong and of a good courage" (Joshua 1:6). In chapter 2 Joshua sends spies ahead to Jericho.

keyFigures.role: Tells Joshua to lead Israel across the Jordan and promises to be with him.

keyFigures.name: Reuben, Gad, and half of Manasseh

keyThemes.explanation: God promises, "the LORD thy God is with thee whithersoever thou goest."
"This book of the law shall not depart out of thy mouth; but thou shalt meditate therein day and night."
The people promise Joshua what they promised Moses.
The eastern tribes must help their brothers, as they promised.

Joshua 2.summary: Joshua secretly sends two spies from Shittim to look over the land, especially Jericho. They lodge at the house of Rahab, a prostitute, whose home is on the city wall (Joshua 2:1-3; Joshua 2:15). When the king of Jericho demands that she hand them over, she hides them under stalks of flax on her roof and tells the king's men they have left (Joshua 2:4-7). She tells the spies that the people of the land are terrified because of what they have heard about the Red Sea and the defeat of Sihon and Og, and she declares that the LORD "is God in heaven above, and in earth beneath" (Joshua 2:8-11). She asks them to spare her family, and they swear to do so if she keeps their mission secret and ties a scarlet cord in her window (Joshua 2:12-21). The spies return and report that the people are melting in fear (Joshua 2:22-24).
Joshua 2.whereWeAre: In chapter 1 Joshua told the people to get ready to cross the Jordan in three days. First he sends two spies to Jericho, where Rahab hides them and asks to be spared. Their report that the land is afraid leads to the crossing in chapter 3.

keyFigures.name: Joshua
keyFigures.role: Sends two spies from Shittim.

keyFigures.name: The two spies
keyFigures.role: Hide at Rahab's house and promise to spare her family.

keyFigures.name: Rahab
keyFigures.role: Hides the spies and confesses that the LORD is God.

keyFigures.name: The king of Jericho
keyFigures.role: Sends men to arrest the spies.

keyThemes.explanation: Rahab says, "the LORD your God, he is God in heaven above, and in earth beneath."
Rahab shows kindness to the spies and asks for kindness in return.
A red cord in the window marks the house that will be saved.

Joshua 3.summary: Early in the morning Israel leaves Shittim and camps at the Jordan. After three days, officers instruct the people: when they see the ark of the covenant carried by the Levitical priests, they must follow it, keeping about two thousand cubits (roughly 3,000 feet) behind, "for ye have not passed this way heretofore" (Joshua 3:1-4). Joshua tells them to consecrate themselves, for the LORD will do wonders (Joshua 3:5). The LORD tells Joshua that he will begin to exalt him in the eyes of Israel (Joshua 3:7). Joshua explains that the living God is among them and will drive out the Canaanite peoples; when the priests' feet touch the water, the Jordan will stop flowing (Joshua 3:9-13). Although the river is at flood stage during harvest, when the priests step in, the water piles up far upstream at Adam, and all Israel crosses on dry ground while the priests stand firm in the riverbed (Joshua 3:14-17).
Joshua 3.whereWeAre: The spies came back from Jericho in chapter 2 saying the people of the land were melting with fear. Now Israel follows the ark to the Jordan, and the river stops flowing so they can cross on dry ground. Chapter 4 tells how they mark the day with twelve stones.

keyFigures.name: Joshua
keyFigures.role: Tells the people to get ready and leads them to the river.

keyFigures.name: The priests
keyFigures.role: Carry the ark into the Jordan and stand in the riverbed.

keyFigures.name: The people
keyFigures.role: Follow the ark and cross on dry ground.

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Stops the river and begins to "magnify" Joshua.

keyThemes.explanation: The ark goes first, a sign that the living God is among them.
"Sanctify yourselves: for to morrow the LORD will do wonders among you."
God begins to "magnify" Joshua, as he did Moses.
The water stops only when the priests' feet touch it.

Joshua 4.summary: After the people cross, the LORD tells Joshua to have twelve men, one from each tribe, take twelve stones from the middle of the Jordan where the priests stood and carry them to the place where Israel will camp (Joshua 4:1-3). The stones are to serve as a memorial: when children later ask what they mean, parents will explain that the Jordan's waters were cut off before the ark (Joshua 4:4-7). Joshua also sets up twelve stones in the middle of the Jordan (Joshua 4:9). About forty thousand armed men cross over before the LORD (Joshua 4:12-13). After all have crossed, the priests come up and the waters return (Joshua 4:15-18). Israel camps at Gilgal, east of Jericho, and Joshua sets up the twelve stones there (Joshua 4:19-20). The purpose is that all the peoples of the earth may know that the LORD's hand is mighty and that Israel may fear him forever (Joshua 4:21-24).
Joshua 4.whereWeAre: Israel has just crossed the Jordan on dry ground in chapter 3. Twelve stones are carried out of the riverbed and set up at Gilgal, Israel's first camp in the land. In chapter 5 Israel prepares there for its first battle.

keyFigures.name: Joshua
keyFigures.role: Sets up twelve stones at Gilgal.

keyFigures.name: The twelve men
keyFigures.role: Carry stones from the middle of the Jordan.

keyFigures.name: The priests
keyFigures.role: Come up out of the river, and the water returns.

keyFigures.name: The men of Reuben, Gad, and Manasseh
keyFigures.role: About forty thousand, who cross over armed for war.

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Dries up the river and tells Joshua to set up the memorial.

keyThemes.explanation: When children ask, "What mean these stones?" parents tell the story.

keyThemes.theme: God's power for all to see
keyThemes.explanation: "That all the people of the earth might know the hand of the LORD, that it is mighty."
The crossing echoes the Red Sea, and the people honor Joshua as they did Moses.

Joshua 5.summary: The kings west of the Jordan hear what the LORD did and lose heart (Joshua 5:1). The LORD tells Joshua to make flint knives and circumcise the Israelites again, because the generation born in the wilderness had not been circumcised (Joshua 5:2-7). The place is named Gilgal, because the LORD says, "This day have I rolled away the reproach of Egypt from off you" (Joshua 5:3; Joshua 5:9). Israel keeps the Passover on the fourteenth day at Gilgal and eats the produce of the land, and the manna stops (Joshua 5:10-12). Near Jericho, Joshua meets a man with a drawn sword who says he has come "as captain of the host of the LORD"; Joshua falls down in worship and is told to remove his sandals because the place is holy (Joshua 5:13-15).
Joshua 5.whereWeAre: Israel is camped at Gilgal after crossing the Jordan in chapters 3–4. Before any battle, the men are circumcised, the Passover is kept, and the manna stops. Then Joshua meets the captain of the LORD's host, and chapter 6 brings the battle for Jericho.

keyFigures.name: The kings of Canaan
keyFigures.role: Hear what God did and lose heart.

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Tells Joshua to circumcise the men.

keyFigures.name: Joshua
keyFigures.role: Circumcises the men and meets the captain of the LORD's host.

keyFigures.name: The new generation
keyFigures.role: Circumcised at Gilgal, they keep the Passover.

keyFigures.name: The captain of the LORD's host
keyFigures.role: Stands with a drawn sword and tells Joshua the ground is holy.

keyThemes.explanation: The new generation is circumcised before its first battle.
Israel keeps its first Passover in the land.
From now on God feeds them from the land itself.
The captain is not for Israel or its enemies, but comes "as captain of the host of the LORD."

Joshua 6.summary: The LORD tells Joshua that Jericho, shut up tight, has been given to him (Joshua 6:1-2). Israel is to march around the city once a day for six days, with seven priests carrying seven rams' horn trumpets before the ark, and on the seventh day march around seven times, then blow the trumpets and shout (Joshua 6:3-5). The city and everything in it is devoted to the LORD for destruction, except Rahab and her household, and the silver, gold, bronze, and iron, which go to the LORD's treasury (Joshua 6:17-19). The people are warned not to take any devoted things. When the people shout, the walls fall, and Israel takes the city (Joshua 6:20-21). Joshua sends the two spies to bring out Rahab and her family, who are spared (Joshua 6:22-25). Joshua pronounces a curse on anyone who rebuilds Jericho (Joshua 6:26), and the LORD's fame spreads (Joshua 6:27).
Joshua 6.whereWeAre: Joshua has just met the captain of the LORD's host near Jericho in chapter 5. Now Israel marches around the city for seven days, and "the wall fell down flat" (Joshua 6:20). Rahab is saved, but chapter 7 reveals that someone has taken what was devoted to God.

keyFigures.role: Gives Joshua the plan and the city.

keyFigures.name: Joshua
keyFigures.role: Leads the march and gives the order to shout.

keyFigures.name: The priests

keyFigures.name: The people
keyFigures.role: March in silence, then shout.

keyFigures.role: Saved because she hid the spies.

keyFigures.name: The two spies

keyThemes.explanation: Marching and shouting could never bring down walls, so the victory is clearly God's.
Everything in Jericho belongs to the LORD.
The woman who trusted God is saved with her family.
"So the LORD was with Joshua; and his fame was noised throughout all the country."

Joshua 7.summary: Israel's victory at Jericho is followed by failure. The text says Israel acted unfaithfully regarding the devoted things, because Achan son of Carmi of the tribe of Judah took some of them, and the LORD's anger burned against Israel (Joshua 7:1). About three thousand men attack the small town of Ai and are routed, with thirty-six killed (Joshua 7:2-5). Joshua tears his clothes and prays in distress (Joshua 7:6-9). The LORD tells him that Israel has sinned and violated the covenant and that he must consecrate the people and find the guilty party by lot (Joshua 7:10-15). The lot identifies Achan, who confesses to taking a beautiful cloak, silver, and a bar of gold and burying them in his tent (Joshua 7:16-21). The items are recovered, and Achan and his family are taken to the Valley of Achor, where they are stoned and burned (Joshua 7:22-25). The LORD's anger turns away (Joshua 7:26).
Joshua 7.whereWeAre: Jericho fell in chapter 6, and everything in it was devoted to the LORD. But Achan secretly took some of it, and Israel is beaten at the small town of Ai. Once the sin is dealt with, chapter 8 tells how Ai is taken.

keyFigures.name: Achan

keyFigures.name: Joshua

keyFigures.name: All Israel

keyThemes.explanation: Achan's secret sin brings defeat on the whole people.
Joshua pours out his confusion before the LORD.
Achan confesses, but judgment still follows.
Joshua asks, "Why hast thou troubled us?" and the place is named the valley of Achor, meaning trouble.

Joshua 8.summary: The LORD tells Joshua not to be afraid and to take all the fighting men against Ai, this time with permission to take the spoil and livestock (Joshua 8:1-2). Joshua sends a force to set an ambush behind the city, then leads the main force forward and pretends to retreat as before. When the men of Ai pursue them, the ambush rises up, enters and burns the city (Joshua 8:3-19). Trapped between the two forces, the army of Ai is destroyed, and the king is captured and hanged on a tree until evening (Joshua 8:20-29). Joshua then builds an altar on Mount Ebal as Moses commanded, offers sacrifices, writes the law on stones, and reads all the words of the law, blessings and curses, in the hearing of the whole assembly, including the women, children, and foreigners (Joshua 8:30-35).
Joshua 8.whereWeAre: Achan's sin was judged in chapter 7. Now God sends Israel against Ai again, and an ambush wins the city. Then Joshua reads the law at mount Ebal, as Moses commanded, before the Gibeonites arrive with their trick in chapter 9.

keyFigures.role: Tells Joshua not to fear and gives him Ai.

keyFigures.name: Joshua

keyFigures.name: The congregation

keyThemes.explanation: God tells Joshua, "Fear not, neither be thou dismayed."
The ambush works because Joshua does what God says.
Joshua reads every word of the law at mount Ebal.
Women, children, and strangers hear the law too.

Joshua 9.summary: When the kings west of the Jordan hear of Israel's victories, they unite to fight (Joshua 9:1-2). The people of Gibeon, however, use deception: they send envoys with worn sacks, patched wineskins, old sandals, and dry, moldy bread, claiming to have come from a far country (Joshua 9:3-13). The Israelite men sample their provisions but do not consult the LORD (Joshua 9:14). Joshua makes a peace treaty with them, and the leaders swear an oath (Joshua 9:15). Three days later Israel learns they are neighbors (Joshua 9:16-17). Because they had sworn by the LORD, the leaders will not harm them, though the people grumble (Joshua 9:18-20). Joshua confronts the Gibeonites, who explain their fear of the LORD's power, and he makes them woodcutters and water carriers for the congregation and the altar (Joshua 9:21-27).
Joshua 9.whereWeAre: Israel has taken Jericho and Ai in chapters 6–8, and the kings of Canaan are joining forces. The people of Gibeon trick Israel into a peace treaty instead. That treaty pulls Israel into the great battle of chapter 10.

keyFigures.role: Join forces to fight Israel.

keyFigures.name: The Gibeonites
keyFigures.role: Trick Israel with old clothes and moldy bread.

keyFigures.name: Joshua
keyFigures.role: Makes peace with them, then makes them servants.

keyFigures.name: The people
keyFigures.role: Grumble against the princes.

keyThemes.explanation: The leaders "asked not counsel at the mouth of the LORD."
Israel keeps its oath even though it was tricked.
The Gibeonites lie because they fear what God will do to them.
The Gibeonites cut wood and draw water for the altar.

Joshua 10.summary: Adonizedek, king of Jerusalem, hears that Gibeon has made peace with Israel and forms an alliance with the kings of Hebron, Jarmuth, Lachish, and Eglon to attack Gibeon (Joshua 10:1-5). The Gibeonites call for help, and Joshua marches all night from Gilgal and surprises the allies (Joshua 10:6-9). The LORD throws the enemy into confusion and sends large hailstones that kill more than the Israelites' swords (Joshua 10:10-11). Joshua prays, "Sun, stand thou still upon Gibeon; and thou, Moon, in the valley of Ajalon," and the sun stands still about a whole day, as the book of Jasher records (Joshua 10:12-14). The five kings hide in a cave at Makkedah and are captured and executed (Joshua 10:16-27). Israel then conquers a series of cities in the south (Joshua 10:28-39), and the chapter summarizes the campaign (Joshua 10:40-43).
Joshua 10.whereWeAre: Israel made peace with Gibeon in chapter 9. Now five Amorite kings attack Gibeon, and Joshua marches all night to defend it while the sun stands still. The southern cities fall one after another, and chapter 11 turns north.

keyFigures.name: Horam king of Gezer

Israel marches to help the city it promised to protect.
"there was no day like that before it or after it."
The southern cities fall one by one.

Joshua 11.summary: Jabin king of Hazor leads a northern coalition of kings with a vast army, horses, and chariots gathered at the waters of Merom (Joshua 11:1-5). The LORD tells Joshua not to fear and that he will hand them over, and to hamstring their horses and burn their chariots (Joshua 11:6). Joshua attacks suddenly and defeats them, pursuing them to Sidon and beyond (Joshua 11:7-9). He turns back, captures Hazor, and burns it, the only city on a mound burned (Joshua 11:10-13). The people take the livestock and plunder but devote the inhabitants to destruction, as Moses commanded (Joshua 11:11-15). The chapter summarizes that Joshua took the whole land, including the hill country, the south, and the valley, and cut off the Anakims (Joshua 11:16-22). No city except Gibeon made peace (Joshua 11:19). The chapter ends, "And the land rested from war" (Joshua 11:23).
Joshua 11.whereWeAre: The south was won in chapter 10. Now Jabin king of Hazor gathers the kings of the north with horses and chariots, and Joshua defeats them at the waters of Merom. The chapter ends, "And the land rested from war" (Joshua 11:23), and chapter 12 lists the defeated kings.

keyFigures.name: The northern kings

keyFigures.name: The LORD

keyFigures.role: Defeats the northern army and burns Hazor.

keyThemes.explanation: God tells Joshua, "Be not afraid because of them."
Israel burns the chariots instead of keeping them.
Joshua "left nothing undone of all that the LORD commanded Moses."
"And the land rested from war."

Joshua 12.summary: The chapter summarizes Israel's victories. First it lists the two kings defeated by Moses east of the Jordan: Sihon king of the Amorites at Heshbon, and Og king of Bashan, whose land was given to Reuben, Gad, and half of Manasseh (Joshua 12:1-6). It then lists the thirty-one kings defeated by Joshua west of the Jordan, from the south (Jericho, Ai, Jerusalem, Hebron, Jarmuth, Lachish, Eglon, Gezer, Debir, and others) to the north (Hazor, Shimronmeron, Achshaph, Taanach, Megiddo, Kedesh, and others), ending with "all the kings thirty and one" (Joshua 12:7-24). Joshua assigned their land to the tribes according to their divisions (Joshua 12:7).
Joshua 12.whereWeAre: The wars that began at Jericho ended in chapter 11. This chapter lists every king Israel defeated, two east of the Jordan under Moses and thirty-one west of it under Joshua. Chapter 13 turns from winning the land to dividing it.

keyFigures.name: Moses and the children of Israel
keyFigures.role: Defeated Sihon and Og east of the Jordan.

keyFigures.name: Joshua and the children of Israel
keyFigures.role: Defeated the thirty-one kings west of the Jordan.

keyFigures.name: Sihon and Og
keyFigures.role: The two kings defeated east of the Jordan.

keyThemes.explanation: The list shows all that God did for Israel.
The victories of both leaders are counted as one story.
Each city is named so the victory will be remembered.

Joshua 13.summary: Joshua is old, and the LORD tells him that "there remaineth yet very much land to be possessed" (Joshua 13:1). The chapter lists the areas still unconquered: the Philistine territory with its five rulers, the Geshurites and others in the south and north, the Canaanite coast and Sidonian territory, and the region of Lebanon (Joshua 13:2-6). The LORD promises to drive them out and tells Joshua to divide the land among the nine and a half tribes (Joshua 13:6-7). The chapter then describes the land Moses had already assigned east of the Jordan: Reuben (Joshua 13:15-23), Gad (Joshua 13:24-28), and the half-tribe of Manasseh (Joshua 13:29-31). It notes that Balaam son of Beor was killed in battle (Joshua 13:22), and repeats that the tribe of Levi received no land inheritance because the LORD is their inheritance (Joshua 13:14; Joshua 13:33).
Joshua 13.whereWeAre: The war chapters ended with the list of kings in chapter 12. Now Joshua is old, and much land is still not taken, but God tells him to divide it among the tribes. This chapter recalls the land already given east of the Jordan, and chapter 14 begins the division west of it.

keyFigures.name: Joshua

keyFigures.name: Reuben, Gad, and half of Manasseh
keyFigures.role: Already have land east of the Jordan.

keyThemes.explanation: The job is not finished, but God promises to drive out the rest.
Each tribe's land is God's gift.
"the LORD God of Israel was their inheritance."

Joshua 14.summary: The chapter opens the account of the allotment of land west of the Jordan. Eleazar the priest, Joshua, and the heads of the tribes distribute the inheritance by lot, as the LORD commanded through Moses (Joshua 14:1-5). Caleb son of Jephunneh, of the tribe of Judah, comes to Joshua at Gilgal and recalls the spying at Kadeshbarnea when he brought back a faithful report, and Moses promised him the land he had walked on (Joshua 14:6-9). Now eighty-five years old and still strong, he asks for the hill country of Hebron, where the Anakims live, saying, "if so be the LORD will be with me, then I shall be able to drive them out" (Joshua 14:10-12). Joshua blesses him and gives him Hebron, because Caleb wholly followed the LORD (Joshua 14:13-14). The land then has rest from war (Joshua 14:15).
Joshua 14.whereWeAre: Chapter 13 described the land given east of the Jordan. Now the division of Canaan begins, and Caleb, the faithful spy of Numbers 14, asks for Hebron at eighty-five. Chapter 15 describes the land of his tribe, Judah.

keyFigures.role: Help Joshua divide the land by lot.

keyFigures.role: Come with Caleb to Joshua at Gilgal.

keyFigures.role: Blesses Caleb and gives him Hebron.

keyThemes.explanation: Caleb's faith forty-five years ago is honored now.
At eighty-five, Caleb asks for the hardest land: "give me this mountain."
What Moses promised, Joshua gives.
Caleb "wholly followed the LORD God of Israel."

Joshua 15.summary: The chapter describes the allotment to the tribe of Judah. The boundaries are traced in detail: the southern border from the Dead Sea (Salt Sea) toward Kadeshbarnea (Joshua 15:1-4), the eastern border along the Dead Sea (Joshua 15:5), the northern border past Jerusalem (Joshua 15:6-11), and the western border at the Mediterranean (the Great Sea) (Joshua 15:12). Caleb receives Hebron and drives out the three sons of Anak, then offers his daughter Achsah as wife to the man who captures Kirjathsepher (Debir); Othniel son of Kenaz takes it (Joshua 15:13-17). Achsah asks her father for springs of water and receives the upper and lower springs (Joshua 15:18-19). The rest of the chapter lists Judah's towns by region (Joshua 15:20-62), and ends by noting that the people of Judah could not drive out the Jebusites living in Jerusalem (Joshua 15:63).
Joshua 15.whereWeAre: Caleb received Hebron in chapter 14. This chapter gives Judah's borders and towns, the first and largest share west of the Jordan. Chapters 16–17 turn to the tribes of Joseph.

Caleb, Othniel, and Achsah each act with courage.

The Jebusites stay in Jerusalem.

Joshua 16.summary: The chapter describes the lot for the descendants of Joseph, whose portion is divided between Ephraim and Manasseh. The southern boundary starts at the Jordan near Jericho and goes up through the hill country to Bethel and westward toward the sea (Joshua 16:1-4). The border of Ephraim is described in more detail, including its southern and northern edges (Joshua 16:5-8). Ephraim is also given towns set apart within the territory of Manasseh (Joshua 16:9). The chapter ends with the note that Ephraim did not drive out the Canaanites living in Gezer, who lived among them and were put to forced labor (Joshua 16:10).
Joshua 16.whereWeAre: Judah's land was described in chapter 15. Now the lot falls to the sons of Joseph, and this chapter gives Ephraim's borders in the middle of the land. Chapter 17 gives the land of Manasseh, Joseph's other son.

Making the Canaanites serve instead of driving them out will bring trouble later.

Joshua 17.summary: The chapter continues the allotment to Manasseh. Machir, Manasseh's firstborn, already received Gilead and Bashan east of the Jordan because he was a man of war (Joshua 17:1). The remaining clans, including Abiezer, Helek, Asriel, Shechem, Hepher, and Shemida, receive land west of the Jordan (Joshua 17:2). The five daughters of Zelophehad (Mahlah, Noah, Hoglah, Milcah, and Tirzah) approach Eleazar and Joshua and remind them that the LORD commanded Moses to give them an inheritance among their brothers, and they receive it (Joshua 17:3-6). The borders of Manasseh are described (Joshua 17:7-11), but Manasseh could not drive out the Canaanites from some cities and put them to forced labor (Joshua 17:12-13). The descendants of Joseph complain that their lot is too small; Joshua tells them to clear the forested hill country and drive out the Canaanites despite their iron chariots (Joshua 17:14-18).
Joshua 17.whereWeAre: Chapter 16 gave Ephraim's land. Now Manasseh receives its share, including the land promised to the daughters of Zelophehad in Numbers 27. When Joseph's tribes complain that their land is too small, Joshua tells them to clear the forest, and chapter 18 moves the camp to Shiloh.

keyFigures.role: Give them their share.

They remind the leaders, "The LORD commanded Moses to give us an inheritance."
Joshua tells Joseph's tribes to clear the forest for themselves.
Canaanites are put to work instead of being driven out.

Joshua 18.summary: The whole congregation gathers at Shiloh and sets up the tent of meeting there, and the land lies subdued before them (Joshua 18:1). Seven tribes have not yet received an inheritance, and Joshua asks, "How long are ye slack to go to possess the land?" (Joshua 18:2-3). He tells each tribe to choose three men to survey the land and write a description of it in seven parts (Joshua 18:4-7). The men go and record the land in a book by towns in seven divisions, and Joshua casts lots for them before the LORD at Shiloh (Joshua 18:8-10). The rest of the chapter describes the allotment of Benjamin, including its borders and towns, which lies between Judah and the descendants of Joseph (Joshua 18:11-28).
Joshua 18.whereWeAre: Judah and the tribes of Joseph received their land in chapters 15–17, but seven tribes still have none. Israel sets up the tabernacle at Shiloh, and Joshua sends men to map the rest of the land. Benjamin's share is given here, and chapter 19 gives the other six.

keyFigures.name: The congregation
keyFigures.role: Gathers at Shiloh and sets up the tabernacle.

keyFigures.name: Joshua
keyFigures.role: Asks how long they will wait and casts lots.

keyFigures.name: The surveyors

keyFigures.name: Benjamin
keyFigures.role: Receives its land between Judah and Joseph.

keyThemes.explanation: The tabernacle is set up at Shiloh, in the middle of the land.
"How long are ye slack to go to possess the land?"
The land is mapped and divided by lot.
The lots are cast "before the LORD."

Joshua 19.summary: The remaining six lots are cast at Shiloh. Simeon receives towns within Judah's territory because Judah's portion was too large (Joshua 19:1-9). Zebulun's lot is in the lower Galilee (Joshua 19:10-16), Issachar's around the Jezreel Valley (Joshua 19:17-23), Asher's along the northern coast (Joshua 19:24-31), and Naphtali's in the upper Galilee (Joshua 19:32-39). Dan's lot lies between Judah and Ephraim near the coast, but the Danites later find it insufficient (Joshua 19:47), go up and fight against Leshem, take it, and rename it Dan after their ancestor (Joshua 19:40-48). The people give Joshua the city he asks for, Timnathserah in the hill country of Ephraim, which he builds (Joshua 19:49-50). The chapter ends, "These are the inheritances, which Eleazar the priest, and Joshua the son of Nun, and the heads of the fathers of the tribes of the children of Israel, divided for an inheritance by lot in Shiloh" (Joshua 19:51).
Joshua 19.whereWeAre: Benjamin received its land in chapter 18. Now the last six tribes receive theirs, and Joshua himself is given a town last of all. With every tribe settled, chapter 20 sets apart the cities of refuge.

keyFigures.name: The six tribes
keyFigures.role: Simeon, Zebulun, Issachar, Asher, Naphtali, and Dan receive their land.

keyFigures.name: The children of Dan
keyFigures.role: Take Leshem and name it Dan.

keyFigures.name: Joshua
keyFigures.role: Builds the city of Timnathserah.

keyFigures.name: Eleazar and the tribal leaders
keyFigures.role: Finish dividing the land at Shiloh.

keyThemes.explanation: Every tribe now has its land.
Simeon's towns lie inside Judah, because Judah's share was too large.
Dan's land is too small, so the tribe takes Leshem.
Joshua takes his own town only after everyone else has theirs.

Joshua 20.summary: The LORD tells Joshua to designate cities of refuge, as spoken through Moses, so that someone who kills a person unintentionally can flee there and be safe from the avenger of blood (Joshua 20:1-3). The fugitive stands at the city gate, explains his case to the elders, and is taken in and given a place to live (Joshua 20:4). If the avenger comes, the elders must not hand him over, because he killed without prior hatred (Joshua 20:5). He remains there until he stands trial before the congregation and until the death of the high priest (Joshua 20:6). Six cities are named: Kedesh in Galilee, Shechem in the hill country of Ephraim, and Kirjatharba (Hebron) in Judah on the west; and Bezer, Ramoth in Gilead, and Golan in Bashan on the east (Joshua 20:7-8). The protection applies to both Israelites and the foreigner living among them (Joshua 20:9).
Joshua 20.whereWeAre: The land was divided among the tribes in chapters 13–19. Now Israel sets apart six cities of refuge, as God commanded Moses. Chapter 21 gives the Levites their towns.

The cities are just what God told Moses.

Joshua 21.summary: The heads of the Levite families approach Eleazar, Joshua, and the tribal leaders at Shiloh and remind them that the LORD commanded that the Levites receive cities with pasturelands (Joshua 21:1-3). The cities are assigned by lot from the other tribes: thirteen cities for the Kohathite descendants of Aaron, ten for other Kohathites, thirteen for the Gershonites, and twelve for the Merarites, totalling forty-eight cities (Joshua 21:4-40). The list includes the six cities of refuge (for example 21:13,21,27,32,36,38). The chapter concludes that the LORD gave Israel all the land he had sworn to their fathers and they took possession of it, that he gave them rest on every side, that none of their enemies stood against them, and that "There failed not ought of any good thing which the LORD had spoken unto the house of Israel; all came to pass" (Joshua 21:41-45).
Joshua 21.whereWeAre: The cities of refuge were named in chapter 20. Now the Levites receive forty-eight towns among the tribes. The chapter ends by saying God kept every promise, and chapter 22 sends the eastern tribes home.

keyFigures.name: Eleazar and Joshua
keyFigures.role: Give them their towns by lot.

keyFigures.name: The children of Israel

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Gives Israel rest and keeps every promise.

keyThemes.explanation: The tribe without land receives towns among all the tribes.
Each tribe gives some of its towns.
"There failed not ought of any good thing which the LORD had spoken."
God gives Israel rest on every side.

Joshua 22.summary: Joshua calls the Reubenites, Gadites, and the half-tribe of Manasseh, commends them for keeping their promises, and sends them home with a blessing and a charge to love the LORD and keep his commandments (Joshua 22:1-9). On the way, they build a large altar at the Jordan (Joshua 22:10). When the rest of Israel hears, they gather at Shiloh to go to war against them (Joshua 22:11-12). First they send Phinehas son of Eleazar the priest and ten chiefs to confront them, accusing them of breaking faith and recalling the sin at Peor and the sin of Achan (Joshua 22:13-20). The eastern tribes reply, calling on the LORD as witness, that the altar is not for sacrifice but a witness that they too belong to the LORD, so that future generations will not say they have no share in him (Joshua 22:21-29). Phinehas and the chiefs are satisfied, and the eastern tribes name the altar Ed, meaning a witness (Joshua 22:30-34).
Joshua 22.whereWeAre: With the land won and divided in chapters 1–21, the tribes from east of the Jordan can finally go home. But the altar they build by the river nearly starts a civil war. In chapter 23 an old Joshua gives his first farewell.

keyFigures.name: Joshua
keyFigures.role: Blesses the eastern tribes and sends them home.

keyFigures.name: Reuben, Gad, and half of Manasseh
keyFigures.role: Build a great altar by the Jordan.

keyFigures.name: The congregation
keyFigures.role: Gathers at Shiloh ready for war.

keyFigures.name: Phinehas

keyFigures.name: The ten princes
keyFigures.role: Go with Phinehas and accept the answer.

keyThemes.explanation: The tribes nearly go to war but talk it through instead.
The western tribes fear that a rival altar will bring God's anger on everyone.
The eastern tribes worry that their children will be cut off from the LORD.
Phinehas hears their answer and is satisfied.

Joshua 23.summary: Long after the LORD has given Israel rest, Joshua, old and advanced in years, summons the elders, heads, judges, and officers (Joshua 23:1-2). He reminds them that the LORD fought for them and will drive out the nations that remain (Joshua 23:3-5). He urges them to be very strong to keep and do all that is written in the book of the law, not to mix with the nations that remain, not to mention or swear by their gods, but to hold fast to the LORD (Joshua 23:6-8). He reminds them that one of them put to flight a thousand because the LORD fights for them, and tells them to love the LORD (Joshua 23:9-11). If they instead ally themselves with those nations by intermarriage, the nations will become snares and traps until Israel perishes from the good land (Joshua 23:12-13). Joshua says he is "going the way of all the earth" and that not one of the LORD's good promises has failed, but the LORD can also bring every evil thing if they break the covenant (Joshua 23:14-16).
Joshua 23.whereWeAre: Years have passed since the tribes went home in chapter 22, and Joshua is very old. He gathers Israel's leaders and warns them to stay faithful and not to mix with the nations that remain. In chapter 24 he gathers all the tribes at Shechem for his final call.

keyFigures.name: Joshua
keyFigures.role: Old, he calls Israel's leaders together and warns them.

keyFigures.name: The elders, heads, judges, and officers
keyFigures.role: Hear his farewell.

keyThemes.explanation: "not one thing hath failed of all the good things which the LORD your God spake concerning you."
"Take good heed therefore unto yourselves, that ye love the LORD your God."
The nations left in the land will become "snares and traps" to Israel.
The God who kept his good promises will also keep his warnings.

Joshua 24.summary: Joshua gathers all the tribes of Israel at Shechem and calls their leaders before God (Joshua 24:1). He speaks for the LORD, recounting Israel's story: Abraham's ancestors served other gods beyond the Euphrates; God called Abraham, gave him Isaac, Jacob, and Esau; led Israel out of Egypt and through the sea; fought for them against the Amorites; turned Balaam's curse into blessing; and gave them a land they did not labor for (Joshua 24:2-13). Joshua calls them to fear the LORD and serve him, putting away other gods, and says, "choose you this day whom ye will serve... but as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD" (Joshua 24:14-15). The people promise to serve the LORD, and Joshua warns them that they are not able, for the LORD is a holy and jealous God (Joshua 24:16-20). They insist, and Joshua makes a covenant with them, writes it in the book of the law, and sets up a great stone as a witness (Joshua 24:21-28). The book closes with the death of Joshua at 110, the burial of Joseph's bones at Shechem, and the death of Eleazar (Joshua 24:29-33).
Joshua 24.whereWeAre: Joshua warned Israel's leaders in chapter 23 to stay faithful. Now he gathers all the tribes at Shechem, retells their story, and calls them to choose whom they will serve. The book ends with Joshua's death, and the story continues in Judges, where Israel soon forgets.

keyFigures.name: The tribes of Israel
